summary: John N. Nassikas, Chairman of the Federal Power Commission, submitted a detailed technical letter commenting on the Draft Environmental Statement for Operation Breakthrough, focusing on total energy systems and fuel cell technology. He noted that total energy systems are not new, have accumulated operating experience, and are not necessarily more efficient than other electrical systems on an annual basis, while also highlighting promising fuel cell research. His comments were informational and technical in nature, neither endorsing nor opposing the project.
complaint_summary: Nassikas raises technical concerns that the Draft Environmental Statement's discussion of total energy systems overstates their novelty and efficiency advantages, noting they are not new, have known design challenges balancing electrical and heat loads, and are not necessarily more efficient than other electrical systems on an annual basis, while also noting promising but unproven fuel cell technology.

statement.text:
This is in reference to your letter of April 9, 1971, requesting comments of the Federal Power Commission on the Draft Environmental Statement, Operation Breakthrough, April 9, 1971.
In accordance with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 and the role of expertise assigned to the Federal Power Commission by the Guidelines of the Council on Environmental Quality dated April 23, 1971, our commerts will be focused as you suggest on the general Breakthrough effort and, as such, will take up the technical characteristics of total energy systems and the environmental consequences of use of such systems in large housing projects. Since your referral speaks for the most part ir generalities, these comments should not be misconstrued as being addressed to specific housing projects briefly mentioned or as related to a detailed analysis as required by Section 102 (2) (C) of the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969.
With regard to Section 5 of the Draft Statement entitled "Advanced Utility Systems Demonstration", pages 21 and 22, it should be noted that there is a body of literature and accumulated operating experience regarding the validity of these systems as elements of design of large housing projects. The Statement also appears to justify support of total energy systems on the ground that such systems contribute to air quality improvement by reducing fuel consumption for required energy demand.
Total energy systems -- those which are designed to generate electricity and to use exhaust heat or steam for hot water heating and space heating and cooling or for process heat -- have been on the industrial scene for many years. More recently oil and gas fueled total energy systems have been designed using diesel, gas turbine or gas engine prime movers to serve apartment complemes, educational institutions, and suburban shopping centers. The 1971 Directory and

Mr. Charles J. Oilebeke
Data Book of Total Energy Magazine lists 507 total energy systems currently in service, of which 428 include generation of electricity in all types of installations. The total installed generating capacity is over one million kilowatts. In Jamacia, New York, the Rochdale Village project has been in operation since Detember 1963. This installation which consists of two 6,000-kilowatt steam turbines, and two 3,000-kilowatt diesel engines serves apartments, shopping centers, and other service buildings. Under construction at the present time is Wingate Village in Indianapolis, Indiana, which when completed will consist of 1,250 apartments whose energy requirements will be provided by eight 500-kilowatt gas-engine generators. Enough design and practical operating experience have been accumulated to demonstrate the technical and economic criteria which must be satisfied before the full potential of the total energy concept can be realized.
To achieve its full economic potential, the heat requirements of the hot water and space heating and cooling components of a total energy system must balance to a substantial degree the heat in the exhaust gases or steam being rejected by the prime mover used in the generation of electricity. If the heat in the exhaust gases or steam is in excess of these requirements at any particular moment, some of the heat must be discarded or stored with a resultant drop in overall efficiency of the system. If the heat in the exhaust gases or steam in storage is not sufficient to match the heat demand for hot water or space heating and cooling or process steam, it is common practice to supply the deficiency from other sources.
It is often difficult to achieve a good balance between electrical and heat loads in a housing project because of the varying demand for electric service during the course of the day and night. Each total energy system is in fact a mini-electric utility system faced with the same problems of diversity of demand, reserve capacity, maintenance of equipment, and equipment breakdowns. But, whereas the central station can depend on the network for assistance in time of trouble, the total energy system usually must rely entirely on its own resources. On the other hand the reliability of a total energy system is not affected by external network disturbances against which electric network utility systems must protect themselves.
While the foregoing discussion is restricted to current technology in the design of total energy systems, it is appropriate in the context of Operation breakthrough's search for innovative methods and procedures to mention current research in fuel cells. In May 1971 an experimental

Mr. Charles J. Onlebeke
prototype total energy fuel cell installation was made in a single family dwelling in Farmington, Connecticut, as part of a nine-year research and development program conducted under the auspices of the Team to Advance Research for Gas Energy Transformation. Present plans are that this installation is to be followed by 31 other installations in various parts of the country and in different applications. Upon the conclusion of this program operating experience should be available to provide a basis of judging the practical and economic feasibility of generating electricity in relatively small fuel cells using natural gas and other suitable substances to provide the input energy.
While it is often unwise to anticipate result of research and development, it is difficult to overlook contagious optimism of fuelcell sponsors or to underestimate the profound changes that could result from successful fuel cell applications or the wide range of benefits which can result from reduction in the number of conventional fossil fuel combustion operations for space heating and electricity generation. A successful fuel-cell module of 10 to 15 kilowatts, envisioned for single family residences, could be coupled in banks to serve larger users. Looking to the larger applications, the fuel cell because of its modular capability and the possibility of tailoring power output to a specific customer's needs, could find broad application in all sizes of commercial and apartment complexes. Since the fuel cell would not be dependent on electric transmission and distribution networks, successful conclusion of the current experiments would permit significant future environmental advantages. Furthermore, fuel cell installations in the future which eliminate the need for a multiplicity of small conventional fuel combustion operations augur well for a general benefaction of air quality in urban centers which are currently faced with difficult air pollution problems.
We have tried to indicate that total energy systems are not new; that considerable experience has been accumulated in the operation of these systems; and that total energy systems are not necessarily more efficient on an annual basis than other electrical systems. We have also noted promising advances which are currently being made in fuel cell technology in application to residential and possibly larger commercial loads.
Sincerely,
John N. Nassikas
